integration.api: SwitchBot Open API (cloud, https://api.switch-bot.com) DOES document the AI Art Frame with three commands: `next`, `previous`, and `uploadImage` accepting {"imageUrl":"https://..."} or {"imageBase64":"data:image/jpeg;base64,..."}. Status fields: battery, displayMode (0=static,1=slideshow), imageUrl, firmware version; webhook 'changeReport'. So programmatic image push IS possible - but every call traverses SwitchBot's cloud with an account token. GitHub issue #461 ('Add support for CRUD image functionality in AI Art Frame in the API') was still open as of 2026-01-08 asking for exactly this, so `uploadImage` appears to be a recent addition; there is still no documented delete/list.

integration.local_push: YES - fully local, and the best in the survey. The vendor ships an MIT-licensed Home Assistant component that connects directly to the device by IP on the LAN, with mDNS discovery or manual IP entry, and no cloud in the path. Images are processed locally (JPEG conversion, optional dithering) and pushed straight to the device. Vendor also advertises a 'Local Desktop App - Cloud-free desktop application for complete privacy'.
integration.api: A machine-readable OpenAPI spec (openapi.yaml) is published in the vendor's own GitHub repo and the API appears UNAUTHENTICATED on the LAN. Paths: GET /deviceInfo, GET /state, POST /show, POST /showNext, POST /sleep, POST /reboot, POST /clearScreen, POST /settings, GET /whistle, POST /upload (single JPEG, multipart/form-data), POST /image/uploadMulti, POST /image/dataUpload (pre-dithered raw data), POST /image/delete, GET /gallery/list, PUT|GET|DELETE /gallery, GET /playlist/list, PUT|GET|DELETE /playlist. SEPARATELY, docs/Schedule_Pull_API.md documents a 'Schedule Pull' mode purpose-built for exactly this use case: you configure the device with PUT /upstream/pull_settings pointing at YOUR server plus a token and a wake time; the device then wakes on schedule, calls your /eink_pull endpoint for an image URL, displays it, and schedules the next wake from your response's next_cron_time, with an optional /eink_signal callback. No BLOOMIN8 cloud is in that loop at all. Constraints on your static server: correct Content-Length, NO chunked Transfer-Encoding, NO gzip Content-Encoding, baseline (not progressive) JPEG, portrait pixel orientation, _P.jpg / _L.jpg filename suffixes.
integration.subscription: None found. Vendor markets buy-once with no fees.
third_party_projects: ARPOBOT-BLOOMIN8/eink_canvas_home_assistant_component (vendor-published, MIT licence, HACS-installable, exposes ~20 services incl. upload_image_url, upload_image_data, upload_images_multi, upload_dithered_image_data, delete_image, show_next, sleep, reboot, clear_screen, whistle, update_settings, and gallery/playlist CRUD)
integration.evidence: Read the vendor's GitHub repo README, its file tree, its openapi.yaml, and docs/Schedule_Pull_API.md directly. This is the only device in the survey where I could read a complete, published local API specification rather than a marketing claim.

devices.art_suitability: Same panel class as the InkPoster Tela 28.5" (2160x3060, 131 ppi, portrait 3:4, Spectra 6 + Sharp IGZO) at the same $2,399 price, but with a documented, unauthenticated local REST API, an MIT-licensed HA component, and a device-pulls-from-your-server scheduling mode. For a self-hosted archive that wants to drive the frame from its own software, this is the reference option. The counterweight is entirely vendor risk, not technical: a six-person startup, and this specific SKU has not shipped yet.

vendors.ownership: Privately held. Verified roll-up: (a) InkPoster is PocketBook's own brand, not a separate company - inkposter.com's about page names 'Pocketbook International SA' and says InkPoster was 'Designed by PocketBook, a Swiss-based global leader... nearly two decades of innovation'; (b) PocketBook acquired IONNYK, announced 2025-09, price undisclosed, IONNYK founders staying on and the Belgian team fully integrated; (c) PocketBook became 'a substantial shareholder and co-owner' of Chinese maker Bigme in 2024.
vendors.funding: No external funding disclosed; self-funded from a long-running e-reader business
vendors.revenue_scale: Not disclosed. Inferable scale: a global e-reader brand shipping since 2012 across the US and EU, now running a five-SKU art-display line from $499 to $6,500 with US and German distribution and free FedEx fulfilment.
vendors.hardware_track_record: Strongest hardware pedigree in the category after SwitchBot: nearly two decades of shipped e-readers, plus co-developed products with Bigme (PocketBook InkPad EO derived from the Bigme InkNote Color+ with PocketBook firmware). Executed the InkPoster launch on time into two major markets and won a German Design Award 2026 for the Tela 28.5".
vendors.abandonment_history: None found for e-readers. Two cautions from this research: the Tela 40.5" and Duna 40.5" have been 'Notify me' since CES 2026, and Engadget reported an April 2026 availability target for the Duna that has visibly slipped by four months; and the InkPoster FAQ pre-announces a future paid subscription, which is a policy-change risk on a device you already own.
vendors.rationale: Second-strongest counterparty. Confirms the brief's suspicion in full and then some: InkPoster, IONNYK and Bigme are all one counterparty, so three apparently independent shortlist entries collapse into a single point of failure. Diversification across those three brands buys nothing. Against that, PocketBook is the only vendor in the category with two decades of e-paper hardware behind it and a real European manufacturing footprint acquired specifically to reduce Asia/US supply dependence. Its weakness for this project is not survival, it is posture: zero developer surface, no API, app-and-account mandatory, and a subscription explicitly on the roadmap.

Proxies from 2022: ~1,000,000 frames sold cumulatively, ~3,000,000 app users, ~100% year-on-year growth for three consecutive years, collectively showing about 1 billion pictures daily. At a $149-$499 ASP that implies a business in the low hundreds of millions cumulative - far larger than the $3.7M 'ARR' figure floated by one revenue-estimate aggregator, which appears to be nonsense and is discarded.
vendors.headcount: Not disclosed in any source I read
vendors.hardware_track_record: Founded as Pushd, renamed Aura before its first frame in 2016; a decade of continuously shipped consumer frames (Carver, Walden, Aspen, Mason and now Ink) sold at retail and through Amazon. Aura Ink shipped on schedule after its 2025-10-21 announcement and remains in stock. The most consumer-credible brand in the category.
vendors.abandonment_history: None found. Aura's standing commitment to unlimited photo storage with no subscription across a decade of frames is the opposite of an abandonment signal, and it is the reason the brand has the reputation it does.

vendors.name: Fraimic
vendors.corporate_form: Private startup; legal entity name not published on the site
vendors.ownership: Founder-owned. CEO Anthony Mattana, described as a Broadway sound designer turned hardware founder.

vendors.hardware_track_record: Mixed but real. Fraimic itself is a first product under its own name. The founder previously ran two Kickstarter hardware campaigns through Hooke Audio (Hooke Verse and Hooke Lav; Hooke Lav hit its $10K goal with $100K in eight hours but ran into pandemic-era parts lead times), and one podcast interview says he sold a previous company to Logitech - I could not verify which company or confirm the Logitech transaction from a primary source. So: a repeat crowdfunding hardware founder who has delivered before, not a first-timer, but not an established manufacturer either.
vendors.abandonment_history: No abandoned product found. Two live warning signs: the May 2026 Kickstarter ship date had no public confirmation of backer deliveries as of 2026-07-27, and the Large Canvas list price rose about 50% from the announced $999 retail to a $1,499 list. Early software shipped buggy on preproduction units (broken dashboard redirects, invalid API endpoints), reportedly fixed quickly.
vendors.rationale: A single-product, first-product company with about $1.1M of crowdfunding, no disclosed institutional backing, an unconfirmed backer-fulfilment record, and a 50% price increase between announcement and shipping. On a three-year horizon this is the highest-risk vendor among the credible >15" options. The mitigation is real but conditional: because the frame is claimed to work fully over the LAN with no server dependency, company death would cost you AI generation and firmware updates but not the device - New Atlas's reviewer made exactly that argument. That mitigation is only worth what the local API is worth, and the local API is asserted by the vendor, corroborated by one reviewer, and documented by nobody.

vendors.name: arpobot (BLOOMIN8)
vendors.country: Australia (Sydney - D9/161 Arthur Street, Homebush West 2140) with a Shenzhen office (307 Chongwen Park, Nanshan District)
vendors.corporate_form: Private startup; no legal entity name published on its about page
vendors.ownership: Founder-owned; the about page pictures six people (Francis as Creator, Eric supply chain, Piper marketing, Evan and Linda engineering)
vendors.funding: Kickstarter A$2,397,443 from 2,272 backers against an A$30,000 goal (7991%), 2025-03-18 to 2025-04-27, average pledge A$1,055; continued afterwards on Indiegogo InDemand. No institutional funding disclosed.
vendors.revenue_scale: Crowdfunding plus DTC; roughly A$2.4M of campaign revenue plus subsequent store sales. Small.
vendors.headcount: Six people pictured on the about page
vendors.hardware_track_record: Two products in three years: the Arpobot Smart Shade in 2023, then the BLOOMIN8 Canvas line. The 7.3" and 13.3" Canvas models are shipping; the 28.5" is the last and largest SKU, expected to start shipping August 2026. So they have demonstrably delivered hardware to backers at the smaller sizes - which is more than Fraimic has publicly confirmed - but the specific in-scope SKU is still unshipped.
vendors.abandonment_history: None found - the company is too young to have one. The relevant durability signal here is different and unusually strong: they publish their device's OpenAPI specification and an MIT-licensed Home Assistant component in a public repo. That means the local control surface survives the company. If arpobot folds, a competent owner can still drive the frame from a self-hosted server using the published spec, and the Schedule Pull mode means the frame is already designed to fetch from your server rather than theirs.
vendors.rationale: As a corporate counterparty this is the weakest credible option: a six-person, three-year-old, crowdfunded startup with no institutional backing. But staying power and openness interact here in a way that matters more than the raw rating. For every other vendor, company death means a bricked or content-starved frame, because the image path runs through their servers. For BLOOMIN8 the image path is documented, unauthenticated, on your LAN, and published under MIT - so vendor death degrades to a hardware-warranty problem rather than a functionality problem. Weigh the low rating accordingly rather than treating it as disqualifying.

leads_not_followed.lead: SwitchBot AI Art Frame undocumented local HTTP endpoints on port 8080. A secondary source states that the pragmatic path for Home Assistant users is 'local network polling via undocumented HTTP endpoints (port 8080), which may break with firmware updates'. I could not confirm this from any primary source, forum thread, or repo.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: If real, it would convert the single strongest-staying-power vendor in the category from 'closed / cloud-required' to 'partly-open', and would make the 31.5" SwitchBot the best combined bet in the survey. This is the highest-value open question remaining. Verify by putting a unit on a LAN and port-scanning it, or by searching the Home Assistant community forum and the switchbot subreddit for 'port 8080'.

leads_not_followed.lead: Fraimic's actual local REST API surface. The vendor advertises a REST API and a local-only mode and exposes https://fraimic.local, but publishes no endpoint reference; the official user manual documents only the cloud path. Kickstarter returns 403 to this tool so I could not read the campaign FAQ where the API may be described.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: Fraimic Large Canvas is the leading candidate on hardware and price, and its entire abandonment-risk mitigation rests on the local API being real and complete. 'Marketing claims a local API' and 'a documented local API exists' are very different purchases. Verify by browsing http://fraimic.local on a unit and enumerating routes, or by asking Fraimic support directly for the API reference.

leads_not_followed.lead: Whether the BLOOMIN8 mobile app / initial provisioning requires an arpobot account or cloud round-trip, even though steady-state control is local. support.bloomin8.com returns 403 to this tool and I could not read the Home Assistant support article or the account/privacy documentation.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: A cloud-mandatory first-boot would mean the device bricks on activation if arpobot disappears before you set it up, undermining the otherwise excellent survives-the-vendor argument. It would also affect whether a second unit could be commissioned years later.

leads_not_followed.lead: Resolution and PPI of the SwitchBot AI Art Frame 31.5". No page I could read states it. The Fraimic and InkPoster 31.5" units are both 2560x1440 at 94 ppi, strongly suggesting a common E Ink 31.5" Spectra 6 module, but I did not verify SwitchBot uses it.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: If SwitchBot's 31.5" is the same 2560x1440 panel, then at $1,299.99 shipping today from a publicly traded vendor it is directly price-comparable to Fraimic's $1,299 and undercuts InkPoster's $1,699 for identical image quality, and the decision reduces cleanly to integration openness versus vendor risk.

leads_not_followed.lead: Six additional colour-ePaper frame brands exhibited at E Ink's photo-frame theme wall at COMPUTEX 2026 that I did not investigate: Aelig, Kokonna, SMARTWIZ+ art, SWISH, YeconTech, and Aipusi (alongside Aura, Bloomin8, InkJoy, PocketBook, Reflection Frame and SwitchBot).
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: One of these could be a >15" entrant nobody has covered. The same source notes the exhibited range spans 7.3" to 40.5" but that '10-inch and 13.3-inch [are] the current mainstream specifications', so the prior is that they are all small - which is why I deprioritised them. Worth a single sweep if the shortlist needs widening.

leads_not_followed.lead: InkPoster Tela 40.5" and Duna 40.5" real ship dates. Both have been 'Notify me' on the vendor's own catalogue for seven months since CES 2026, and the Duna's Engadget-reported April 2026 availability has slipped by four months with no public explanation.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: These are the only >40" colour options in existence. If they ship, they change the top of the market; if the slip continues, the practical ceiling for a colour art wall stays at 31.5". Worth a direct sales enquiry rather than more web research.

leads_not_followed.lead: Whether any of the 28.5"/31.5" frames can be driven at native resolution without the vendor's dithering pipeline. Fraimic (proprietary dithering), Aura (proprietary dithering algorithm), and InkJoy (ISFR engine) all promote in-house image processing; BLOOMIN8 alone exposes an /image/dataUpload endpoint accepting pre-dithered raw data.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: For an art archive, colour fidelity on a 6-ink panel is decided almost entirely by the dithering algorithm. The ability to supply your own pre-dithered data - which only BLOOMIN8 documents - means you can tune reproduction per artwork rather than accepting the vendor's generic photo-optimised pipeline. This may matter more to final image quality than the ppi differences between devices.

leads_not_followed.lead: Visionect (Slovenia) 32" Place & Play e-paper display, positioned as digital signage rather than art.
leads_not_followed.why_it_matters: A >15" reflective e-paper device from a company with a long B2B track record and, being a signage product, likely a far more open management/API story than any consumer art frame. It is monochrome and not marketed as art, so it falls outside the literal scope, but as a self-hosted-archive display it may be a better engineering fit than several in-scope consumer frames. I did not research it.

unverified_facts.claim: SwitchBot AI Art Frame can be controlled locally over HTTP on port 8080 without the SwitchBot cloud.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: Asserted by a single secondary aggregator page that surfaced in search results. No primary source, no repo, no forum thread, and no vendor documentation corroborates it. I did not read the page it came from and am not citing it. Treat as rumour until tested on hardware.

unverified_facts.claim: The SwitchBot AI Art Frame 31.5" uses a 2560x1440 panel at ~94 ppi.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: Inferred from the fact that both other 31.5" Spectra 6 art frames (Fraimic Large Canvas and InkPoster Affresco 31.5") independently specify 2560x1440 at 94 DPI, implying a single E Ink module. No SwitchBot page I could read states any resolution for the 31.5" model.

unverified_facts.claim: Anthony Mattana (Fraimic CEO) sold a previous company to Logitech.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: Stated in a podcast show-notes page, which did not name the company. His documented prior venture is Hooke Audio. I found no filing, press release, or Logitech announcement confirming an acquisition, and no source connecting him to the 2014 Hush smart-earplug campaign despite the surface similarity.

unverified_facts.claim: IONNYK Linn and Maxine display diagonals are 31.2" and 40.2" respectively.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: Computed by me from the display AREAS published on ionnyk.com (69 x 39 cm and 82 x 61 cm). IONNYK publishes frame dimensions and display areas but never a diagonal or a resolution, and I could not reach any retailer spec sheet (luxuryformen returns 403). Published secondary figures for these frames are unreliable - one roundup reports IONNYK sizes by taking the frame dimensions as the screen.

unverified_facts.claim: Aura Frames has raised USD 46.9M lifetime over 8 rounds and has 125 employees; and separately, that its revenue is USD 3.7M ARR.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: Both come from data-aggregator pages (Tracxn, GetLatka) that appeared in search results and that I did not fetch. The $3.7M revenue figure is flatly inconsistent with ~1M frames sold at $149-$499 and is very likely wrong. The verified figure is ~USD 39M raised as of the 2022 TechCrunch round.

unverified_facts.claim: MelonFrame's largest model is 13.3" and Memoir's three sizes are all under 15".
unverified_facts.why_unverified: Neither vendor publishes a screen size anywhere I could read, including MelonFrame's own support pages. Kickstarter returns 403 to this tool. The 13.3 diagonals recorded for both are upper-bound inferences from price points ($99 and $149 entry) and from the fact that the E Ink consumer frame market's stated mainstream sizes are 10" and 13.3". They are not measurements.

unverified_facts.claim: InkJoy Frame will be offered in a size larger than 13.3".
unverified_facts.why_unverified: The vendor says only that 'multiple frame sizes will be available' and publishes no list. I could not fetch the Kickstarter campaign (403) or the one review carrying specs (content truncated). The 13.3 recorded is an assumption, not a fact.

unverified_facts.claim: Fraimic Large Canvas units are actually in customers' hands.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: Three sources disagree as of early August 2026: Forbes (2026-07-21) says 'shipping now'; fraimic.com's product page says 'Ships Early August'; the shop collection shows both SKUs 'Sold out'; and BackerGuardian (2026-07-27) found no public confirmation of any backer delivery against a promised May 2026 date. The only reviewed unit anywhere was a preproduction 13.3". No independent confirmation of a delivered 31.5" exists.

unverified_facts.claim: The BLOOMIN8 local REST API is genuinely unauthenticated on the LAN.
unverified_facts.why_unverified: The published openapi.yaml declares no security scheme and the HA component README documents no authentication, which together strongly imply an open endpoint - but absence of a declaration in a spec is not proof of absence in firmware, and the Schedule Pull configuration does involve a token for the upstream direction. Confirm on hardware before designing around it, and note that an unauthenticated endpoint is itself a LAN security consideration for the installation.

unverified_facts.claim: PocketBook International SA is the direct legal owner of the IONNYK entity (as opposed to an affiliate or holding company being the acquirer).
unverified_facts.why_unverified: The acquisition is well documented in PocketBook's own announcement and in trade press, but no source I read named the acquiring legal entity or disclosed the transaction structure or price. The InkPoster-to-PocketBook relationship IS directly verified (inkposter.com's about page names Pocketbook International SA).
